utterances.text: That was an electric substation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we continue, please? Can we stop for a moment? Sir, the field we have just seen, was that part of the school complex as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were prisoners kept on any portion of that field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, prisoners were kept both in the building that we saw and on that field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of shelter, if any, did the prisoners who were kept in the field have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the prisoners would make themselves, improvise tents from materials that they had available, blankets, pieces of plastic sheeting. They improvised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The building which is seen in the upper right portion of the screen now -- yes, if we could move forward just slightly -- what is that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It also belonged to these grounds before the war. Before the war it housed a cinema, and in this front part there was a small bar and to the side up there were also the offices of the Local Commune, yes, of the Local Commune.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that building used as part of the Trnopolje camp during its operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and inmates were also put in there, but I mean women and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it used by camp officials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a room in the middle part where these vaults are there, that office was also used by the Serb Red Cross as their office and the Camp Commander and personnel head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the offices of the Serb Red Cross located within that building during the entire operation of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, a major part of them were here, but later on they moved to a building across the street from this building where before the war there was also, there had also been a small restaurant, a coffee bar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we continue with the video, please? Can we stop here? What do we now see on the screen, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this point we also see the building where there was a store from the south, from the southern side, and here we also see the building of this surgery, of this outpatient facility, where we worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the medical clinic you referred to is in that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for orientation, the school building is beyond this building, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can continue, please? Does this show the school field on which prisoners erected makeshift shelters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is where they were but on the rear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stop here. The building in the picture now, the two buildings in the picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is again the school building, its southern view, and to the left on the screen is the gymnasium and to the right is the school building. In the middle was the southern school entrance with the boiler room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continue, please. Stop here. What are we now seeing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now we see the building which housed the cinema in Trnopolje, the former cinema, which showed films and during the war it was also used to keep prisoners, detainees, and women and children prepared for deportation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can continue? Stop here. As the camera panned back, it was paning in the direction of the railroad station, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, this would indeed be a new Exhibit and it would be No. 296.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to 296?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 296 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sir, you referred earlier to the guards. Did guards at Trnopolje camp work in shifts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the guards worked in shifts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many guards were in each shift?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were about 50 guards in every shift, especially in the beginning, plus at the very outset they were reinforced with some combat units, a relatively small group of men who remained there only for a short while, and only those guard shifts looking after the camp remained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the official explanation by camp officials for why Muslim men, women and children had been gathered, collected, at Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the beginning, in those early days, the Serb soldiers used to tell us that we were there so that they, the Serb Army, could protect us against the Muslim extremists, as they put it, so as to protect us, so as to shield us from their attacks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were the Muslims of Kozarac or Trnopolje or Prijedor or Hambarine in danger of attack by Muslim extremists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no way. I mean, something like that could never happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did a Serbian television crew come to the camp and do some filming there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, once a TV crew from Banja Luka came to the camp, and they wanted to show their viewers how the Serb Army was protecting, protected the Muslim people. So soldiers were assigned to individual points and at that moment they began firing and taking up positions. Of course, the camera was shooting it all, and this was to be proved that they were protecting us and that the camp was being attacked by Muslims, that is, that the Muslims were attacking their own people, other Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before assuming these positions and beginning the shooting, had the guards or Serbian soldiers consulted with the TV crew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. One director, presumably, of the whole enterprise, he assigned various soldiers to various positions, changed them, shifted them around, indicated them in what direction they should run or lie down, in what direction to fire and so on and so forth. So they made a dress rehearsal and then they really started shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there ever an attack on Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, instead of protection from attack or protection of Muslim people from attack by Muslim extremists, what was Trnopolje camp used for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically, the Trnopolje camp was used for the ethnic cleansing of the Kozarac area of the domicile Muslim population. It was something like a point where the civilian population, men, women and children, would be gathered, collected, and thence on deported to other parts of Bosnia or other territories. Practically, so like a collection point, but also to destroy the Muslim population, since many were killed in that camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did camp officials ever explicitly say whether Muslims would be allowed to remain in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, once I was on the Red Cross premises where the camp Commander was and he said during that conversation with his associates that only a small number, that those people who had no houses of their own which had been destroyed, they would be deported, and that others would remain. But after that he said, "10 per cent of the Muslims may stay here, others have to go out".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who said that 10 per cent of the Muslims may stay in Prijedor but the others would have to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They must disappear, that was the camp Commander who said that, Mr. -- Major Kuruzovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you later hear from other Serb officials that there was some problem or disagreement with even this limited number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from a Serb soldier we learnt subsequently that a large number of the population had already been deported, that some political structures were against even this low percentage and that they should be reduced to two per cent of the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were local Serbian civilians or others discouraged from helping Muslims who were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, later on while the camp was in existence, the local, some individual, local Serbs tried to help their neighbours, Muslims. I remember an elderly woman who brought food to her Muslim neighbour, but the guards then intervened quite rigorously and they turned her back home, threw that food on the ground. But the next day she came again and then they again interfered rigorously, the same thing happened and, as we learnt, they fired at her house saying that she was a traitor. Moreover, we also learned from other Serbs that they were forbidden to communicate with Muslims, to talk to them, and that those found out would be punished or some other sanctions would be used against them or, rather, that they could either lose their jobs or, if they were male, they would be sent to the front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did someone associated with the Red Cross, the Serbian Red Cross, come to the camp in the first few days of its operation and bring some milk for babies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a Serb, who was among the executive staff of the Red Cross in Prijedor, used to bring us in the beginning a small quantity of milk powder for the infants in the camp. Evidently, one of those military executives did not like it. So, as he was going back to Prijedor, he was stopped at a military checkpoint and beaten up there. He automatically lost his job and replaced by another man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who replaced him or who the head of the Serbian Red Cross was during the bulk of the operation at Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was replaced by Pero Curguz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that the former head had brought small quantities of milk for the infants. Approximately, how many infants, that is, under the age of one year old, were in Trnopolje camp in its early stages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they distributed that milk, they had a record 800 infants, that is, new borns below the age of one. Mothers had to bring the infants there and write down their full name, and only then they got that milk and then he said, "We have distributed 800 packages".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there attempts by Muslims who had not been brought to the camp to assist those who were confined in the camp, and did those sometimes provoke violent reactions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in those early days of the camp, the population who were in their homes around Trnopolje also tried to somehow get the food to us, give the food to the inmates, but they refused that, they abused verbally those people who were bringing that food, and driving them away from the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall an occasion where a Muslim male brought money for the purpose of purchasing bread for the prisoners of Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a Muslim, at some point a Muslim brought 1,000 German marks to the Serb Red Cross. He denoted that money, asking that the Red Cross organise the delivery of bread from Prijedor to all those people who were in the camp. They took the money. We never got that bread. That man was taken to the office and was interrogated and severely beaten. He was really very badly battered. After that he was detained in a room in our laboratory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions about the general conditions of Trnopolje camp, but before I do, I want to refer back to your explanation that Trnopolje was used as a place for deportation. In what ways were prisoners from Trnopolje deported or expelled? How were they collected and removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the surrender of Kozarac itself, the orders came for the civilian population to be collected in the stadium or, rather, in front of the school in Kozarac, and there they separated men from women and then directed them down the road in the direction of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There ----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you, that was unclear question. I apologise. The question I was asking is once people were collected in Trnopolje camp how were they removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, right. People were deported from Trnopolje by railway, that is, in railway carriages. They were taken to there under custody to the station and there ordered to board the carriages. Of course, those were civilian population, women and children. From there, they were taken in the direction of Banja Luka and further on, but at that moment we did not know where they were being taken to. Part of the population was also deported by trucks and buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that a portion of those who were deported after being in Trnopolje camp were removed by rail. Were people put in passenger wagons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- no, no. These were cattle wagons or for any kind of bulk cargo. They were not passenger carriages. They were closed freight carriages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you estimate how many prisoners were deported by freight cars or cattle cars at any given time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to these people's statements, they had very little space, so that a number of them could fit into a car, 100 to 150, but they really were pressed one against the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have an opportunity to count the number of cattle cars or freight cars which were used on a train which deported people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, once I managed to get off to follow those civilians to the station itself, and in that particular convoy, in that train included 27 cars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the deportations by rail or by truck or by bus follow the cleansings of villages and hamlets in the area of Kozarac and Trnopolje and the municipality of Prijedor generally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these trains were organised at certain time intervals, prior to that the population in the neighbourhood, in those villages, individual villages, was collected, that is, as the Serb soldiers put it, they were cleansed. They would come with an APC and with special police troops from Prijedor and they would enter, they would surround it, they would be deployed around the area. They wanted to expel. They would then enter houses, breaking in, firing off and if they would find somebody they would say he immediately had to get out. They were forcing people out, and if anyone managed to take any of their personal effects, that was already a success. Of course, during those sweeping operations some people were even killed if they came across them. The population was fearing for their life, though, were fleeing towards Trnopolje because those were the orders, flee towards Trnopolje, and when they arrived to Trnopolje, they were more often than not separated from other inmates, usually in the cinema hall. Then the next day or that same day or, perhaps, for another day or two, they awaited the transportation and then they were transported further on in the manner I have already described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did traumatized victims of this kind of cleansing seek you out in the medical clinic for either counselling or some kind of medication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, people were panic stricken, in a shock, under a severe stress. Many saw their nearest of kin being killed then or how their houses were set on fire because there was arson as well and, of course, they were experiencing and feeling it all. They came to us asking for our help, for medicines, for advice what to do. They were in a very bad -- in a terrible mental condition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you a few questions about the general conditions in the camp, if I may. First of all, did the camp officials provide the prisoners with food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in Trnopolje there was no organised food distribution by the camp management.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did prisoners feed themselves? What did they do for food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the beginning people ate what they had brought from home in their bags, if they had managed to take something away. After that, we lived on the aid of the local population, of the neighbours, those who had some relatives or somebody to bring them something. Later on, when that population was expelled, the inmates were compelled to go out of the camp for a brief period of time. In the beginning, we called it "going to take a swim", then looked around the gardens for vegetables, for green fruit and anything they could find in those abandoned houses. The remains of whatever they could find, some flour, perhaps, or anything eatable, and they would then bring it to the camp and we prepared the food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it dangerous, using your expression, to "take a swim", that is, to go out and look for food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was terribly dangerous. Even the Serb soldiers on guard themselves and others, other Serbs, in the neighbourhood also rammed those houses, looted, plundered valuables, and they would come across our inmates, so that many were harassed. Some of them were, regrettably, liquidated as well as they went out in search of food. Later on, in the later days of the camp, as people had to go further and further away from the camp, and that was very dangerous indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the hygienic conditions in Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hygienic conditions were horrible. When we arrived in the camp, the school building still had running water from the local system, but in those first days it was turned off so that the hygienic conditions deteriorated in that regard. So that people were forced to go to just one source of water which was across from the main entrance to the school complex. The toilets that were used during that period of time, given the amount of people, got clogged up very fast. The piping was plugged up and many could not get there so that they were forced to go to the toilet outside. We managed to organise through the digging of some improvised toilets which could be used only during the day. In other words, during the night nobody could move outside or else they would be shot at by the guards who were guarding. So that people would go to the toilet next to the door or near the wall, and this contributed to outbreak of diseases. There was a very acute case of dysentery. We had no detergents, no soaps, nothing. People, I remember when I passed through the camp and surveyed the situation, people were lining up in front of the toilets and as they were finished, they would have to go to the back of the line because they knew that they would have to go to the toilet. So a lot of people were unable to control it, so that they, sort of, relieved themselves right there on the spot. So that was horrible. We had patients who were coming and looking for help and often times we could not help. We had nothing to give them. They had blood in their stool. They were losing blood and that, obviously, contributed to a general deterioration of their physical mass. There was not enough food so people were really deteriorating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the children of the camp particularly vulnerable to diseases such as dysentery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, children were practically the target from the very start. They were -- the diarrhoeas led to the loss of water and electrolysis and young bodies showed that very fast. They brought us -- they were bringing us these children, and we tried to help as much as we could, almost half dead. We would give them some kind of syrups. It was horrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What percentage of people in the camp would you estimate suffered from dysentery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My free estimate, I am sure in 95 per cent. I know of very few cases of people who said that they did not have dysentery. We all had it though to a degree, but most, as I said, at least 95 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other diseases or medical problems in the camp resulting from the malnutrition and the lack of hygiene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very soon we had lice and also scabies which is a very uncomfortable disease which we just could not eradicate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the effect of scabies on the body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first, the basic symptom is irritation on different parts of the body. People almost are trying to kind of remove their skin because of the irritation, so that they would injure them -- they would create open wounds that would get infected very fast, so that we had local carbuncles and ferbuncles(?), pus, which was a big problem. We had no antibiotics so that bacteria spread very fast through the bloodstream into other parts of the body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the light of the number of people who suffered from dysentery, did you request that toilet facilities be reinstated or expanded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in conversation with the Serbian Red Cross, we asked that new toilets be made outside, and to clean out the septic holes and to unplug the sewer system as well as to let the running water back into the school, so that we could help improve the hygiene. However, that was refused. They said that the water system was affected, so they did not do it. Two or three times later, some trucks came from Prijedor. They cleaned out those holes but then -- that was a period when we had a lot of rainfall. So it filled up again. Then in the surrounding wells, their disease control service came and they put something in it. We did not know what it was. So people did not dare drink water from those wells, because they feared they might be contaminated or even poisoned which we thought was a real possibly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in addition to the general conditions which you partially described, were prisoners in Trnopolje camp beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the first night you were there was a group of men brought to the camp and beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that first night we were locked up in the clinic and then after, some time after midnight a group of young men was brought in. They were lined up in front of the clinic. They were shouting at them, they were yelling. Then they drove them in with rifle butts. They threatened them and cursed them. After about five or 10 minutes they took them in the direction towards the movie theatre on the south side of the camp. I do not know what happened to those people. The next day I asked the inmates that were around there in that area of the camp, and they said that that night nobody went among, nobody joined the rest of the inmates that night. They were taken somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear any officials from the camp or guards make reference to what happened to those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, several days later one of the prisoners tried to get out through the fence near the gate and I was around there. The guard turned him back asked him: "Where are you trying to go? Do you want ..." He tried to explain to him where he was going and what he wanted and he said, "Go back, or else you will be eaten by fish like those from a few days ago."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By "eaten by fish" was he referring to the nearby fish ponds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from that statement of his one could infer, he sort of smiled cynically, but I understood it to mean, as if they meant, as if those people were taken to that fish pond and that they were killed there and were thrown in there as fish food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were many of those prisoners who were beaten held, in what part of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People who were found in the camp in various places were brought to the commune centre. Sometimes they were interrogated, sometimes they were beaten, and then they would be brought to the room which was our former laboratory and some were then, some would be continuously interrogated or beaten there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the extent of the beatings suffered by some of the prisoners who were brought to the lab?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Given that the laboratory was next to the clinic, we practically shared the entrance. We could see who was being brought in. Also the windows were open, so that we could hear those terrible sounds, those screams, those wails of victims, of beatings. On the other hand, the curses of the Serb soldiers who were beating them, we felt horrible at that moment, we felt helpless. There was nothing we could do and they would continue to beat them. This would happen very often. They would beat them with all kinds of objects, with rifles, pieces of furniture. They would stab them with knives, fists, feet, especially later. After that torture when we came into the laboratory we saw a lot of blood, on the walls, on the floor, imprints of their boots, a horrible sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attempt to treat or assist in the treatment of some of these beaten prisoners and what kinds of injuries did they suffer as a result of the beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Naturally, we always tried to reach those people who were detained there. Sometimes we would succeed. Sometimes, unfortunately, we did not. When we succeeded in begging the Commander or a guard who was in front, then we would see different injuries. I remember what first comes is those dark bruises, the back, in the kidney area, then lacerations on the face. Then we had a patient who had peeled off a part of the scalp. It was hanging, you could see the bone, and he also had the left knee pierced through. Later I would also see another man with a similar wound, except on both knees. They apparently told him to cross legs, because the Muslims especially sit that way, and then with a bayonet they would pierce through the knee. So that those people during that wounding have damage of nerves. So this patient of ours remained an invalid, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see a prisoner with a cross carved on his body, cut into his body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that prisoner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to being taken to the lab for beatings, were male prisoners sometimes called out of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon? I did not ----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were some prisoners simply called out of the camp and removed from Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that also happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did prisoners make an effort to determine what had happened to these prisoners, where they had gone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, usually the procedure was such that people were being called out by name and last name. They were the guards, shifts two and three, they had a list of names and they would go around the camp and they would ask. Of course this was over a period of time. Sometimes smaller, sometimes larger groups of men were taken away. Obviously, we asked about them. What captured my attention was that very often people who were called out would not appear in no other camp, another camp such as Omarska, Keraterm or Manjaca. A very small number that we know showed up there, many of them did not. Many of them were taken away and disappeared, and many of them we do not know about until today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the fate of some of the prisoners who were called out of Trnopolje learned when their bodies had to be buried by other prisoners near Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. People would go out to the vicinity of the camp, they would find the bodies of those people in the fields, behind hedges, in the ravines, and then they would report it to us or to others, to the guards. Then in some cases the command of the camp assigned some people to go and bury those bodies. So that the fate of a smaller number of people whom we recognised is known to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any groups of people who were taken out and whose bodies were found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one of those people who was digging, who was burying the dead, later told me in the camp that they buried the Foric's, those were six young men, related, who were taken out of the camp one afternoon by a policeman. Apart from that, they buried two other men Ante and a Zoran who were from Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there groups of people buried whose names were not necessarily known?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, some groups of people were found later when they were already decomposing, so that they would collect them into a common grave and they would bury them there. You could not recognise or do anything else. There is a mass grave near there with 15, one with 16 such corpses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two separate ones, one with 15 corpses and another one with 16?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did some of the people who were forced to bury these victims come to the clinic for medication or counselling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they came. Usually they would come five or six days later and they were threatened not to talk about it, who they saw and what they did, because they would be killed too. However, in them it created tension. It was the first time for some of them that they had to deal with corpses at all. It was especially terrible that these corpses were decomposing, so there was a stench and they could not bury it, that psychological tension, those nightmares they had during the night. In the end they decided to come to us and ask for help because they trusted us, that we would not tell anything. We would give them tablets to quieten them down. We tried to talk to them, to direct them so they would forget that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned lists from which people were called out. Were some of those lists created within the camp, within Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know who wrote those lists, of course, but it is a fact that I saw those lists from people who were in the management of the camp and from those guards. Also the Red Cross had a list, a census of all men who were in the camp at that time. It was said that who did not report and was in the camp was going to be killed. Everybody had to be registered. They were making, but of course there were other kinds of lists. They were all being recorded into one big ledger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there occasions when people from outside the camp came to the camp to provide lists, either of people to be called out or to be compared against the list which had previously been prepared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that happened on numerous occasions. I saw twice or more a police vehicle, a van, with a policeman who would come to the camp with a such a list, and the deputy commander would come, Slavko Puhalic. He would give him the paper. They would comment on it. They were looking at them. Then Slavko would give that list to the Shift Commander and then he together with the soldiers, with the guards, would go to the camp and was looking for people from those lists, and when they were found they would be taken into the van and driven off. That would repeat several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Deputy Commander Puhalic sometimes come to the clinic with lists of names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he also came to us. Probably he had some information or assumed that we could know some of these people. I was also asked specifically about some. He would sit with us at the table and he would look at the list. We could also see it. It was a list of names lined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the camp authorities such as Puhalic or Major Kuruzovic maintain contact with Serbian officials in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a day when you were taken to the Crisis Staff in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the Crisis Headquarters, namely, one of the guards got sick. In fact he got a seizure and was brought to us, to the clinic, and we gave him first aid. Then they told us that we had to go together with this man to the hospital in Prijedor as his escort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About what time of the day was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was morning, early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you transported to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went by bus of the -- it is a local bus from Prijedor, a city bus, which had brought the Red Cross people. There was no other vehicle at that time. Every morning they would bring the Red Cross. So in that bus with an escort we were taken to the neurological ----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that bus driven by a Serbian soldier or driver who was at the camp all the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a bus driver who was dressed in civilian clothes, but was not a part of the guard in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he would regularly bring members of Serbian Red Cross to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were finished at the hospital did the driver want to take you back to Trnopolje, back to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he refused to go back to Trnopolje. There was a little quarrel with our escort who was there. Then the escort said, "So what shall we do here in Prijedor? We have to go back." The driver said: "I am taking you to the crisis centre in Cirkin Polje, then they can do whatever they want with you", and that is exactly what he did. We got off the bus and the soldier escorted, took us into a garage with a guard who was there at that moment who was guarding that object at the time, and he went into the crisis centre himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After a period of time waiting there, which officials of the Trnopolje camp came out of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After about an hour or two of wait the guard said, "Come out", and when we came out at the door in that moment there was a camp Commander Slobodan Kuruzovic and Slavko Puhalic's deputy, two twin brothers who were Balaban, they were escorts to the Commander -- no. That was all. That was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they take you back to Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Commander, everybody had their own vehicles individually, and the camp Commander said, "You are coming with me". We climbed into his car and he took us towards Trnopolje. He talked a little.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until Tuesday. As I indicated, we will not be hearing this case tomorrow because of another matter that we need to handle. Thank you. We will be adjourned until Tuesday at 10 a.m. (5.30 p.m.) (The court adjourned until Tuesday, 6th August 1996) 24
